lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Eduarda | Lesson 28 -- Term Sheets and LOIs

listenings.text: Hi Eduarda, it's James. NorthPack's letter of intent just arrived, with a two-page term sheet. The headline is good: a purchase price of one hundred and five million, and a closing date at the end of March. But there are two points that we need to push back on. First, they want to keep ten million in escrow for eighteen months, because of the supplier case. I think twelve months is enough. Second, the indemnity cap is twenty percent of the price, which is high for a deal like this. Ten percent is normal. Please walk Victor through the whole document before Thursday, and remember: he shouldn't sign anything until our lawyers have read it. Thanks.

When you read a term sheet, the first question is simple: which parts are binding? Usually, most of a term sheet is not binding. The price, the escrow and the warranties can still change in the final contract. But a few clauses are binding from the day you sign. The most common ones are exclusivity, which means that the seller may not talk to other buyers for a period, and confidentiality, which means that neither side may share the terms. Then look at the small words. Shall and must mean that something is an obligation. May means that something is allowed. And is entitled to means that someone has a right. Read those words slowly, because one small word can change who pays.

extra_audio.text: NorthPack finished the first two weeks of due diligence in the data room. Then Sarah Kim sent a letter of intent with a two-page term sheet. Victor was worried about the ten million in escrow. Eduarda explained that the money comes back after eighteen months. She also told him that the indemnity has a cap of twenty percent. They decided to ask NorthPack for a lower cap before signing.
